Under the hood

It's just arithmetic on a million little numbers.

Tonebox does no magic. Every edit reads the image as a flat array of red, green, blue and alpha bytes, runs some math, and writes the result back with putImageData. This page walks through exactly what that math is — point adjustments, color-space conversions, convolution kernels and the histogram.

Try it in the editor → See the sample gallery

Non-destructive

Sliders never touch the original pixels. Every change recomputes the whole image from the pristine source, so any adjustment can be dragged straight back to zero.

Real convolution

Blur, sharpen, edge-detect and emboss run a genuine NxN kernel over every pixel, sampling neighbours and clamping at the image edges — no CSS filter shortcuts.

Live histogram

After each edit the RGB and luma distributions are counted into 256 buckets per channel and drawn to a canvas, so you can watch tones shift as you work.

1. The image is an array

A canvas ImageData object holds one Uint8ClampedArray. For a W × H image it has W × H × 4 entries — four bytes per pixel in the order R, G, B, A, row by row from the top-left. The "Clamped" part matters: any value you write outside 0…255 is automatically pinned to the nearest valid byte, which saves a lot of manual clamping (though we still clamp explicitly where intermediate math can overflow).

To get the value of pixel (x, y) you compute its base index i = (y * W + x) * 4, then read data[i], data[i+1], data[i+2] for red, green and blue.

2. Point adjustments

A point operation maps each pixel using only its own value — no neighbours involved. Tonebox runs them in a fixed order so they compose predictably:

  • Exposure / gamma raises each channel to a power: out = 255 · (in / 255) ^ γ. We precompute a 256-entry lookup table so the expensive pow only runs 256 times, not once per pixel.
  • Brightness simply adds a constant to every channel.
  • Contrast pushes values away from (or toward) the mid-gray pivot 128 using the classic factor (259·(c+255)) / (255·(259−c)).
  • Temperature & tint nudge the red/blue balance (warm ↔ cool) and the green/magenta balance.
  • Grayscale, sepia, invert, threshold are all mixes toward a target — luma, a sepia matrix, the inverse, or pure black/white — so the slider can sit anywhere between off and full.

Luma — the "brightness" of a pixel

Several filters need a single brightness number for a color. We use the Rec. 601 weighting, which matches how the eye perceives each channel:

Y = 0.299·R + 0.587·G + 0.114·B

Green dominates because our eyes are most sensitive to it; blue barely counts. The same formula feeds the threshold filter and the luma histogram.

3. Hue & saturation live in HSL

You can't rotate a hue by adding to RGB. Instead Tonebox converts each pixel to HSL (hue, saturation, lightness), changes hue or saturation there, then converts back:

  • Hue rotate adds degrees to H and wraps around the 360° color wheel.
  • Saturation multiplies S, clamped to 0…1, so colors get more vivid or wash out to gray.

The conversion is only done when hue or saturation is actually non-zero — otherwise we skip it entirely to keep dragging other sliders fast.

4. Convolution kernels

A convolution replaces each pixel with a weighted blend of itself and its neighbours. The weights form a small grid called a kernel. For a 3×3 kernel we visit the 9 pixels around the target, multiply each by its weight, sum them, divide by a normalizing divisor, and optionally add a bias.

Two details make it correct: we read neighbours from an untouched copy of the source (so a pixel we already changed doesn't pollute the next one), and at the borders we clamp the sample coordinate to the edge instead of reading off the image.

Kernels Tonebox ships

121 242 121

Gaussian blur — neighbours are averaged with the center weighted highest, then divided by 16. Softens noise and detail.

0−10 −15−1 0−10

Sharpen — amplifies the center and subtracts its neighbours (divisor 1), so edges and fine texture pop. The weights sum to 1, keeping overall brightness steady.

−2−10 −111 012

Emboss — a directional gradient with a +128 bias so flat areas become mid-gray and edges turn into raised/recessed ridges.

Sobel edge detection

The edge-detect filter is special: it runs two kernels — one finding horizontal change (Gx), one vertical (Gy) — on the luma of the image, then combines them as magnitude = √(Gx² + Gy²). Bright pixels in the result mark where the image changes fastest: the outlines of objects. The Inkline preset chains Sobel with an invert to give dark lines on white, like a pen sketch.

5. Building the histogram

A histogram counts how many pixels fall at each brightness level. Tonebox keeps four arrays of 256 integers — red, green, blue and luma. It walks the (already edited) pixel buffer once, incrementing red[R], green[G], blue[B] and luma[Y] for every pixel.

To draw it we map each bucket to an x-position and its (log-scaled) count to a bar height. In RGB mode the three channels are painted with the screen blend mode so overlapping regions brighten toward white — exactly how a camera's RGB histogram reads. A histogram bunched on the left means a dark image; pushed right means bright; a narrow spike means low contrast.

A histogram is just a tally (live demo)

Each bar is one brightness bucket; taller means more pixels at that tone. This demo is generated in code on page load.

6. Why this is hard in a page builder

None of this fits a block-based CMS. There is no "Sobel" block, no slider that re-reads a million bytes 60 times a second, no canvas history stack. Tonebox is a single-purpose application — state, a render loop, pixel buffers and an undo tree — that happens to live at a URL. That's the whole point of the demo.
